disease.inheritance: Maternal UBE3A allele loss — paternal allele is imprinted (silenced) in neurons; 15q11-q13 deletion or UBE3A mutation on the maternal chromosome
disease.mechanism: Haploinsufficiency via imprinting. In neurons, the paternal UBE3A allele is normally silenced by genomic imprinting, so only the maternal allele is expressed. Loss of the maternal allele (deletion, mutation, or paternal uniparental disomy) leaves neurons with no functional UBE3A. This is a loss-of-function, but the fix is NOT to add enzyme — it is to UNSILENCE the intact paternal allele.
disease.autotac_rationale: NOT eligible. Angelman is a loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency disease — UBE3A is absent, not accumulated. Degrading any residual UBE3A would worsen the disease. The correct route is to UNSILENCE the intact paternal UBE3A allele (the paternal copy is present but epigenetically off).
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 12,000-20,000 — commonly cited; UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: 6-12 months (developmental delay, ataxia, seizures, happy demeanor)
investigational: Antisense oligonucleotides to unsilence paternal UBE3A (e.g. targeting UBE3A-ATS antisense transcript — clinical)

disease.human_summary: Angelman syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss of the maternal UBE3A allele, leaving neurons without UBE3A because the paternal allele is normally silenced by imprinting. It causes severe developmental delay, ataxia, seizures, and a characteristic happy demeanor. The therapeutic frontier is antisense-mediated unsilencing of the intact paternal allele.
